item.text:
Joe Biden was the U.S. president in 2022. Formally, his office is Article II executive power, commander-in-chief authority, and appointment/enforcement power, but the real 2022 constraint set was Congress, the Supreme Court, federalism, inflation, and midterm politics. I treated your local prior as the fixed structured base and did not re-search those supplied facts.

**Retained source set**
1. [The Constitution of the United States: A Transcription](https://www.archives.gov/founding-docs/constitution-transcript) — National Archives, page last reviewed Feb. 6, 2026. Precise fact: Article II vests executive power in the president, while Articles I and III and the amendments create checks and balances. Period fit: constitutional baseline for all 2022 judgments. Ruler attribution: institutional, not personal. Limitations: legal text only, no performance evidence. Contrary point: it defines power, but not how much Biden could actually get done.

2. [Inaugural Address](https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/inaugural-address-53) — American Presidency Project, Jan. 20, 2021. Precise fact: Biden frames the presidency as democratic restoration after pandemic and Jan. 6. Period fit: baseline mandate for the 2022 year. Ruler attribution: direct presidential self-description. Limitations: rhetorical and self-justifying. Contrary point: later approval data and the midterms show the public mandate was much weaker in practice.

3. [Address Before a Joint Session of the Congress on the State of the Union](https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/address-before-joint-session-the-congress-the-state-the-union-28) — American Presidency Project, Mar. 1, 2022. Precise fact: Biden highlights Ukraine, democracy, inflation, and a domestic recovery agenda. Period fit: central 2022 framing speech. Ruler attribution: direct presidential agenda setting before Congress. Limitations: speech, not implementation. Contrary point: the Court and midterms later narrowed the room he had to act.

4. [Remarks on Signing the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act and an Exchange With Reporters](https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/DCPD-202200559) — GovInfo, June 25, 2022. Precise fact: Biden signs the first major federal gun reform in decades after Uvalde. Period fit: major 2022 domestic-policy event. Ruler attribution: direct executive action. Limitations: the law is narrower than advocates wanted. Contrary point: the underlying gun-violence problem remained severe.

5. [President Biden signs the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 at a White House ceremony on August 9, 2022](https://www.commerce.gov/media/7371) — U.S. Department of Commerce, Aug. 9, 2022. Precise fact: Biden signs the bipartisan semiconductor/industrial-policy bill. Period fit: supply-chain and industrial strategy event in 2022. Ruler attribution: direct presidential enactment. Limitations: implementation is slow and indirect. Contrary point: it does not itself resolve inflation or broader manufacturing decline.

6. [Remarks on Signing Legislation To Combat Inflation, Promote Clean Energy Production, and Reduce Prescription Drug Costs](https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/DCPD-202200712) — GovInfo, Aug. 16, 2022. Precise fact: Biden signs the Inflation Reduction Act. Period fit: one of the year’s signature domestic policy events. Ruler attribution: direct executive action. Limitations: the law’s effects are gradual and the name overstates immediate inflation impact. Contrary point: critics reasonably say it was not a fast inflation-fix.

7. [Statement on the 2022 Congressional Elections](https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/statement-the-2022-congressional-elections) — American Presidency Project, Nov. 16, 2022. Precise fact: Biden accepts Republican control of the House and says he will work with House Republicans. Period fit: key constraint update at the end of 2022. Ruler attribution: direct presidential response to electoral loss. Limitations: self-framing after defeat. Contrary point: the House GOP majority was narrow and often internally unstable.

8. [Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/21pdf/19-1392_6j37.pdf) — U.S. Supreme Court, June 24, 2022. Precise fact: the Court overrules Roe and returns abortion regulation to elected representatives. Period fit: major 2022 constitutional shock and policy constraint. Ruler attribution: external judicial check. Limitations: not a Biden-specific act. Contrary point: it shows the limits of presidential power over constitutional outcomes.

9. [West Virginia v. EPA](https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/20-1530) — Cornell Legal Information Institute, June 30, 2022 decision page. Precise fact: the Court curtails EPA generation-shifting authority under the Clean Air Act. Period fit: major 2022 climate/governance constraint. Ruler attribution: external judicial check on the executive branch. Limitations: agency authority case, not a direct assessment of Biden. Contrary point: the administration still retained other climate tools.

10. [Department of Defense Releases its 2022 Strategic Reviews – National Defense Strategy, Nuclear Posture Review, and Missile Defense Review](https://www.defense.gov/News/Releases/Release/Article/3201683/department-of-defense-releases-its-2022-strategic-reviews-national-defense-stra/?idU=1) — U.S. Department of Defense, Oct. 27, 2022. Precise fact: the 2022 Nuclear Posture Review says nuclear weapons deter nuclear attack and would only be considered in extreme circumstances. Period fit: strongest 2022 source family for Chapter 1B/nuclear context. Ruler attribution: institutional defense doctrine under Biden. Limitations: strategy, not outcomes. Contrary point: doctrine and modernization do not prove effective restraint or success.

11. [Biden Job Approval Dips to New Low](https://news.gallup.com/poll/395378/biden-job-approval-dips-new-low.aspx) — Gallup, July 29, 2022. Precise fact: 38% approve, 59% disapprove. Period fit: public-standing constraint during the 2022 cycle. Ruler attribution: independent polling. Limitations: snapshot poll, not issue-specific. Contrary point: approval is noisy and not a direct measure of competence.

12. [Consumer Price Index News Release - 2022 M12 Results](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/cpi_01122023.htm) — U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Jan. 12, 2023. Precise fact: CPI-U fell 0.1% in December, but rose 6.5% over the prior 12 months. Period fit: best end-of-year inflation readout for inherited conditions in 2022. Ruler attribution: official independent statistics, not presidential narrative. Limitations: aggregate macro data, not causation. Contrary point: inflation was already easing by year-end, so the 2022 picture is not one-way.

**Compact event map**
- Jan. 20, 2021 to Mar. 1, 2022: Biden enters office with a restoration frame, then uses the State of the Union to pivot to Ukraine, inflation, and domestic recovery.
- June 24, 2022: Dobbs overturns Roe, sharply changing the political and legal environment.
- June 25, 2022: Bipartisan Safer Communities Act becomes a real legislative win after Uvalde.
- June 30, 2022: West Virginia v. EPA narrows executive climate leverage.
- Aug. 9, 2022: CHIPS and Science Act signed, a supply-chain and industrial-policy win.
- Aug. 16, 2022: Inflation Reduction Act signed, the largest domestic legislative accomplishment of the year.
- Oct. 27, 2022: DOD releases the 2022 strategic reviews, including the Nuclear Posture Review.
- Nov. 8 to Nov. 16, 2022: midterms produce divided government, with Biden publicly accepting a Republican House.
- Dec. 2022 to Jan. 2023: inflation remains elevated enough to define the year’s inherited economic environment, even as monthly momentum improves.

**Chapter source plan**
- 1B: use the DOD 2022 Nuclear Posture Review, SIPRI 2022 nuclear-force chapter, and FAS 2022 NPR analysis. This chapter is about nuclear posture, not moral credit.
- 2B: use the State of the Union, Ukraine-related official statements, and the local UCDP/SIPRI facts you already supplied. This chapter is about conflict exposure and security context, not automatic ruler attribution.
- 3B: keep the local CIRIGHTS/PTS/V-Dem/UCDP priors as the backbone. Add only sparse narrative sources where needed for ruler attribution and contemporaneous context.
- 4B: use the local Freedom House/V-Dem/RSF/WGI priors as the main evidence, with the State of the Union and the 2022 elections statement for political-rights and checks-and-balances context.
- 5B: use the local Maddison/WDI/UNDP priors, plus the BLS CPI and the major domestic-law signings, for macro scale and policy response.
- 6B: use the local WHO/UNDP priors, plus the CPI and major health/economic legislation, for welfare baselines and policy context.
- 7B: use the local WGI/V-Dem priors, plus Dobbs and West Virginia v. EPA, for accountability, corruption, and rule-of-law constraints.
- 8B: use the local governance-capacity priors, plus the midterms statement, Gallup approval, and the DOD strategic reviews, for implementation capacity and political leverage.
